title: Front, middle and back office: where you fit
story: Welcome to your first day at **Northbridge Energy Trading**, the (fictional) trading desk of a large energy group. Your mentor **Sam**, head of middle office, gives you a coffee and draws three boxes on a whiteboard: *"Before you learn any market, you must know who does what here, and why we never mix the roles."*
objective: I can name the three offices of a trading floor, explain what each one does, and say why middle office must be independent.

write.heading: 1. Why a trading department?
write.body: An energy major produces, buys, refines and sells oil, gas and power. Its trading arm moves these flows to the best market, protects the group against price moves (**hedging**) and takes limited positions to make a profit.

write.heading: 2. The three offices
write.body:
- **Front office**: traders and originators. They decide and enter trades. Goal: make profit within their limits.
- **Middle office**: independent control of the front office. Checks trades, calculates the daily **P&L** (profit and loss) and risk, monitors **limits**, explains P&L changes.
- **Back office** (operations): confirms trades with the counterparty, organises delivery, sends invoices, pays and receives cash.

write.heading: 3. The golden rule
write.body: **Segregation of duties**: the person who makes a trade must never be the person who checks it. Middle office reports to Risk or Finance, not to the traders. Without it, one trader can hide losses (Société Générale, 2008: €4.9 bn loss).

write.heading: 4. Key words
write.body:
- **P&L**: profit and loss, calculated every day.
- **Limit**: the maximum risk a trader is allowed to take.
- **Counterparty**: the company on the other side of the trade.

check.q: Name the three offices and give one task for each.
check.a: Front office: decides and enters trades. Middle office: checks trades, calculates daily P&L and risk, monitors limits. Back office: confirms trades, organises delivery, invoices and settles cash.

check.q: Why must middle office be independent from the traders?
check.a: Because the person who makes a trade must not be the one who checks it (segregation of duties). If traders controlled their own numbers, they could hide losses or take too much risk.

check.q: Who reports to whom: does middle office report to the head of trading?
check.a: No. Middle office typically reports to Risk or Finance, outside the trading line, to stay independent.

read_more:
In the real world, TotalEnergies' trading activity sits in its **Trading & Shipping** organisation, with major hubs in **Geneva** (crude oil and refined products) and **London** (gas, LNG and power). Job titles vary between companies: you may also see *product control*, *risk control*, *trading control* or *valuation control* for tasks that belong to middle office. In all of them, the core is the same: **independent numbers, every day**.

**Tip for your workbook**: write the date and the lesson number at the top of each page, and leave a small box at the bottom of the page for your answers to the questions.
